claim: Dendritic and axonal arbors of many neuronal types exhibit self-avoidance, in which branches repel each other.
source: Dendritic and axonal arbors of many neuronal types exhibit self-avoidance, in which branches repel each other.
evidence: This is a general statement about self-avoidance that is supported by citations to prior work in the Introduction section.

claim: In some cases, neurites interact with those of neighboring neurons, a phenomenon called self/non-self discrimination.
source: In some cases, these neurites interact with those of neighboring neurons, a phenomenon called self/non-self discrimination.
evidence: This statement is supported by references to prior literature and is established knowledge in the field.

claim: In SACs, both self-avoidance and self/non-self discrimination are mediated by the gamma-protocadherins (Pcdhgs), a family of 22 recognition molecules.
source: In SACs, both processes are mediated by the gamma-protocadherins (Pcdhgs), a family of 22 recognition molecules.
evidence: This claim is supported by prior work from the authors (Lefebvre et al., 2012) as cited in the manuscript.

claim: SACs form autapses when self-avoidance is disrupted.
source: SACs form autapses when self-avoidance is disrupted and fail to form connections with other SACs when self/non-self discrimination is perturbed.
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data presented in Figure 3 showing autaptic currents in Pcdhg0 SACs.

claim: SACs fail to form connections with other SACs when self/non-self discrimination is perturbed.
source: SACs form autapses when self-avoidance is disrupted and fail to form connections with other SACs when self/non-self discrimination is perturbed.
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data presented in Figure 4 showing reduced connectivity in Pcdhg1 SACs.

claim: Pcdhgs are required to prune connections between closely spaced SACs.
source: Pcdhgs are also required to prune connections between closely spaced SACs.
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data in Figure 2 showing that connections between closely spaced SACs persist in Pcdhg0 retinas but are eliminated in wild-type retinas.

claim: Alterations in self-avoidance, self/non-self discrimination, and synapse elimination degrade the direction selectivity of DSGCs.
source: These alterations degrade the direction selectivity of DSGCs.
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data in Figures 6 and 7 showing reduced direction selectivity in vDSGCs from Pcdhg0 and Pcdhg1 retinas.

claim: Self-avoidance, self/non-self discrimination, and synapse elimination are essential for proper function of a circuit that computes directional motion.
source: Thus, self-avoidance, self/non-self discrimination, and synapse elimination are essential for proper function of a circuit that computes directional motion.
evidence: This claim is supported by the experimental data showing that perturbations in these processes lead to degraded direction selectivity.

claim: Self-avoidance has been observed in sensory neurons of leech (Hirudo medicinalis), moth (Manduca sexta), fruit fly (Drosophila melanogaster), worms (Caenorhabditis elegans), and zebrafish (Danio rerio).
source: Although not all neurons exhibit self-avoidance, this phenomenon has been observed in a variety of systems including sensory neurons of leech (Hirudo medicinalis; in which the process was first described), moth (Manduca sexta), fruit fly (Drosophila melanogaster), worms (Caenorhabditis elegans), and zebrafish (Danio rerio) (Nicholls and Baylor, 1968; Yau, 1976; Kramer and Kuwada, 1983; Kramer and Stent, 1985; Grueber et al., 2001, 2003; Liu and Halloran, 2005; Sagasti et al., 2005; Smith et al., 2012).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to prior literature.

claim: Dendrites of olfactory projection neurons and axons of mushroom body neurons exhibit self-avoidance in Drosophila.
source: Dendrites of olfactory projection neurons and axons of mushroom body neurons also exhibit self-avoidance in Drosophila (Wang et al., 2002a; Zhan et al., 2004; Hattori et al., 2007).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to prior literature.

claim: Self-avoidance has been documented in cerebellar Purkinje cells and some types of retinal horizontal, bipolar, amacrine, and ganglion cells in mammals.
source: In mammals, self-avoidance has been documented in cerebellar Purkinje cells and some types of retinal horizontal, bipolar, amacrine, and ganglion cells (Montague and Friedlander, 1991; Wassle et al., 2009; Lefebvre et al., 2012; Matsuoka et al., 2012).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to prior literature.

claim: Several cell-surface proteins have been implicated in self-avoidance, including Dscam1, Turtle, Flamingo, LAR-like receptor tyrosine phosphatase, Unc-5, Unc-6 (Netrin), and Unc-40 (DCC) in invertebrates.
source: Several cell-surface proteins have been implicated in self-avoidance, including Dscam1, Turtle, Flamingo, LAR-like receptor tyrosine phosphatase, Unc-5, Unc-6 (Netrin), and Unc-40 (DCC) in invertebrates (Baker and Macagno, 2000; Gao et al., 2000; Matthews et al., 2007; Long et al., 2009; Smith et al., 2012)
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to prior literature.

claim: Several cell-surface proteins have been implicated in self-avoidance in mice, including Dscam, DscamL1, Slit, Robo, Sema6A, PlexA4, PlexA2, and gamma-Protocadherins (Pcdhgs).
source: and Dscam, DscamL1, Slit, Robo, Sema6A, PlexA4, PlexA2, and gamma-Protocadherins (Pcdhgs) in mice (Fuerst et al., 2008, 2009; Lefebvre et al., 2012; Matsuoka et al., 2012; Sun et al., 2013; Gibson et al., 2014).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to prior literature.

claim: Molecules mediating self-avoidance appear to act through contact-dependent repellent mechanisms.
source: In each case, they appear to act through contact-dependent repellent mechanisms.
evidence: This claim is based on inference from prior literature about the mechanisms of self-avoidance molecules.

claim: Fly Dscam1 and mouse Pcdhgs mediate both self-avoidance and self/non-self discrimination.
source: Of the molecules that mediate self-avoidance, two have also been shown to mediate S/NSD: fly Dscam1 and mouse Pcdhgs (Hattori et al., 2007; Hughes et al., 2007; Matthews et al., 2007; Soba et al., 2007; Lefebvre et al., 2012).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to prior literature.

claim: Alternative splicing of Dscam1 transcripts leads to >10,000 recognition units.
source: Alternative splicing of the Dscam1 transcripts and alternative promoter choice (Figure 1B) plus isoform multimerization of Pcdhgs lead to >10,000 recognition units (Schmucker et al., 2000; Tasic et al., 2002; Murata et al., 2004; Schreiner and Weiner, 2010; Thu et al., 2014).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to prior literature.

claim: Alternative promoter choice plus isoform multimerization of Pcdhgs lead to >10,000 recognition units.
source: Alternative splicing of the Dscam1 transcripts and alternative promoter choice (Figure 1B) plus isoform multimerization of Pcdhgs lead to >10,000 recognition units (Schmucker et al., 2000; Tasic et al., 2002; Murata et al., 2004; Schreiner and Weiner, 2010; Thu et al., 2014).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to prior literature.

claim: Each Dscam1 and Pcdhg isoform binds homophilically, but does not bind appreciably to other, closely related isoforms.
source: Second, each Dscam1 and Pcdhg isoform binds homophilically, but does not bind appreciably to other, closely related isoforms (Wojtowicz et al., 2004, 2007; Schreiner and Weiner, 2010; Thu et al., 2014).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to prior literature.

claim: Each neuron in a population expresses a small randomly selected subset of Dscam1 or Pcdhg isoforms.
source: Finally, in those cases where tests have been made, each neuron in a population expresses a small randomly selected subset of isoforms (Neves et al., 2004; Zhan et al., 2004; Kaneko et al., 2006; Miura et al., 2013; Toyoda et al., 2014)
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to prior literature.

claim: Molecular diversification of Drosophila Dscam1 is important for proper patterning of neural circuits.
source: leading to molecular diversification that, in the case of Drosophila Dscam1, has been demonstrated to be important for proper patterning of neural circuits (Hattori et al., 2009).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to prior literature.

claim: SACs provide the principal inhibitory input to ON and ON-OFF direction-selective retinal ganglion cells (DSGCs).
source: SACs also provide the principal inhibitory input to ON and ON-OFF direction-selective retinal ganglion cells (DSGCs) and are essential for their direction selectivity (Yoshida et al., 2001).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to prior literature.

claim: SACs are essential for the direction selectivity of DSGCs.
source: SACs also provide the principal inhibitory input to ON and ON-OFF direction-selective retinal ganglion cells (DSGCs) and are essential for their direction selectivity (Yoshida et al., 2001).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to prior literature.

claim: Individual SAC dendrites are inhibitory direction-selective subunits that wire asymmetrically to DSGCs.
source: Elegant structural and functional studies have revealed the principal elements of the underlying mechanism: individual SAC dendrites are inhibitory direction-selective subunits that wire asymmetrically to DSGCs and inhibit these ganglion cells when visual motion is presented along their proximo–distal axis (Euler et al., 2002; Fried et al., 2002; Briggman et al., 2011; Vaney et al., 2012).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to prior literature.

claim: SAC dendrites inhibit DSGCs when visual motion is presented along their proximo–distal axis.
source: individual SAC dendrites are inhibitory direction-selective subunits that wire asymmetrically to DSGCs and inhibit these ganglion cells when visual motion is presented along their proximo–distal axis (Euler et al., 2002; Fried et al., 2002; Briggman et al., 2011; Vaney et al., 2012).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to prior literature.

claim: The preferred direction of motion for the DSGC is opposite to the preferred direction of motion for the SAC dendrites that innervate it.
source: Thus, the preferred direction of motion for the DSGC is opposite, the preferred direction of motion for the SAC dendrites that innervate it (Figure 1E).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to prior literature and illustrated in Figure 1E.

claim: SACs form inhibitory synapses onto each other.
source: In addition, SACs form inhibitory synapses onto each other, and it has been suggested that these connections sharpen the directional preference of SAC dendrites and thus the directional preference of the DSGCs that they innervate (Lee and Zhou, 2006; Enciso et al., 2010; Taylor and Smith, 2012).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to prior literature.

claim: SAC-SAC connections sharpen the directional preference of SAC dendrites and thus the directional preference of the DSGCs that they innervate.
source: In addition, SACs form inhibitory synapses onto each other, and it has been suggested that these connections sharpen the directional preference of SAC dendrites and thus the directional preference of the DSGCs that they innervate (Lee and Zhou, 2006; Enciso et al., 2010; Taylor and Smith, 2012).
evidence: This claim is based on suggestions from prior literature, indicating it is a hypothesis supported by citations.

claim: Pcdhg-deficient SACs exhibit a dramatic loss of self-avoidance but maintain overlap with neighboring SACs.
source: Pcdhg-deficient SACs exhibit a dramatic loss of self-avoidance but maintain overlap with neighboring SACs, as if they mistake their own dendrites for those of their neighbors and fail to repel them.
evidence: This claim is supported by prior work from the authors (Lefebvre et al., 2012) as cited in the manuscript.

claim: Forcing all SACs to express the same single Pcdhg isoform restores self-avoidance to individual cells but decreases the overlap between neighboring cells.
source: In contrast, forcing all SACs to express the same single Pcdhg isoform restores self-avoidance to individual cells but decreases the overlap between neighboring cells, as if they mistake dendrites of these neighbors for their own and repel them (Figure 1F–H).
evidence: This claim is supported by prior work from the authors (Lefebvre et al., 2012) and illustrated in Figure 1F-H.

claim: In the absence of self-avoidance, SACs will form synapses with themselves (autapses).
source: These results lead to three specific hypotheses about circuit function: (1) in the absence of self-avoidance, SACs will form synapses with themselves (autapses)
evidence: This is a hypothesis that is tested and supported by experimental data in Figure 3.

claim: When S/NSD fails, SACs will form few synapses with each other.
source: (2) when S/NSD fails, SACs will form few synapses with each other
evidence: This is a hypothesis that is tested and supported by experimental data in Figure 4.

claim: Loss of self-avoidance or S/NSD will degrade the direction selectivity of DSGCs.
source: (3) loss of self-avoidance or S/NSD will degrade the direction selectivity of DSGCs.
evidence: This is a hypothesis that is tested and supported by experimental data in Figures 6 and 7.

claim: GABAergic synapses exist between SACs shortly after eye-opening in rabbits.
source: Zheng et al. (2004) demonstrated the presence of GABAergic synapses between SACs shortly after eye-opening in rabbits.
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to prior literature.

claim: Similar SAC-SAC connections occur in young mice.
source: To begin this study, we confirmed that similar connections occur in young mice and asked whether they persist in adults.
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data presented in Figure 2.

claim: SAC-SAC connections persist in adult mice.
source: To begin this study, we confirmed that similar connections occur in young mice and asked whether they persist in adults.
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data presented in Figure 2.

claim: SACs release both GABA and acetylcholine.
source: In addition to releasing GABA, SACs also release acetylcholine, the only retinal neuron to do so (Hayden et al., 1980; Famiglietti, 1983)
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to prior literature.

claim: SACs are the only retinal neuron to release acetylcholine.
source: In addition to releasing GABA, SACs also release acetylcholine, the only retinal neuron to do so (Hayden et al., 1980; Famiglietti, 1983)
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to prior literature.

claim: The dendritic radius of SACs in living tissue is ∼100 µm and varies little between P15 and P100.
source: the dendritic radius of SACs in living tissue is ∼100 µm and varies little between P15 and P100 (Figure 2—figure supplement 1A,B).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data presented in Figure 2—figure supplement 1A,B.

claim: Stimulation of a SAC elicited an inhibitory current in a neighboring SAC in some but not all pairs tested at P15-24 and P40-100.
source: Stimulation of a SAC elicited an inhibitory current in a neighboring SAC in some but not all pairs tested at P15-24 and P40-100 (Figure 2B,C).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data presented in Figure 2B,C.

claim: SAC-SAC currents occurred with a latency of ∼7 ms and averaged ∼15 pA in connected cells at both P15-24 and P40-100.
source: Currents occurred with a latency of ∼7 ms and averaged ∼15 pA in connected cells at both ages (Figure 2J).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data presented in Figure 2J.

claim: SAC-SAC currents were blocked by 50 µM picrotoxin and reversed at the chloride reversal potential, indicating that they were GABAergic and inhibitory.
source: They were blocked by 50 µM picrotoxin and reversed at the chloride reversal potential for our recording solutions (∼–70 mV), indicating that they were GABAergic and inhibitory (Figure 2—figure supplement 2A–C).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data presented in Figure 2—figure supplement 2A–C.

claim: SAC–SAC connections have no significant cholinergic component after eye opening.
source: Although SAC–SAC connections have a cholinergic component before eye-opening in both rabbits and mice (Zheng et al., 2004; Ford et al., 2012), they exhibited no significant cholinergic component after eye opening (data not shown).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data (not shown) and citations to prior literature.

claim: At P15-24, pairs of SACs were over twice as likely to be connected if they were separated by 35–100 µm than if they were separated by 100–175 µm.
source: At P15-24, pairs were over twice as likely to be connected if they were separated by 35–100 µm than if they were separated by 100–175 µm (Figure 2F,K, left).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data presented in Figure 2F,K.

claim: The distance-dependence of SAC-SAC connectivity mirrors the inverse relationship of the distance between SACs and the overlap of their dendritic arbors.
source: This difference mirrors the inverse relationship of the distance between SACs and the overlap of their dendritic arbors (Figure 2—figure supplement 1C).
evidence: This claim is based on inference from the data and geometric considerations illustrated in Figure 2—figure supplement 1C.

claim: Connections were seldom detectable between pairs of SACs separated by <100 µm in adults.
source: In contrast, connections were seldom detectable between pairs separated by <100 µm in adults.
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data presented in Figure 2G,K.

claim: The frequency of connections between pairs of SACs >100 µm apart did not change significantly with age.
source: The frequency of connections between pairs >100 µm apart did not change significantly with age (Figure 2G,K, right)
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data presented in Figure 2G,K.

claim: Synapses between closely spaced SACs are eliminated as SACs mature.
source: The most parsimonious explanation for this difference is that synapses between closely spaced SACs are eliminated as SACs mature.
evidence: This claim is an inference based on the experimental data showing age-dependent changes in connectivity.

claim: Deletion of Pcdhgs leads to excessive cell death in many retinal neuronal populations, but not in SACs.
source: Moreover, deletion of Pcdhgs leads to excessive cell death in many retinal neuronal populations, but not in SACs (Lefebvre et al., 2008, 2012).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to prior work from the authors.

claim: No alterations were observed in the density of SACs or of other retinal cells in Pcdhg0 retinas.
source: As expected, we observed no alterations in the density of SACs or of other retinal cells in Pcdhg0 retinas.
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data presented in Figure 2—figure supplements 3, 4.

claim: The laminar position and mosaic spacing of SACs did not differ detectably between Pcdhg22 and Pcdhg0 retinas.
source: We further verified that the laminar position and mosaic spacing of SACs, as well as overall retinal structure, did not differ detectably between Pcdhg22 and Pcdhg0 retinas (Figure 2—figure supplements 3, 4).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data presented in Figure 2—figure supplements 3, 4.

claim: At P15-24, the number and strength of SAC–SAC connections were similar in Pcdhg22 and Pcdhg0 retinas.
source: At P15-24, the number and strength of SAC–SAC connections were similar in Pcdhg22 and Pcdhg0 retinas: in both genotypes, connections were over twice as common in closely spaced pairs than in pairs separated by >100 µm and current sizes did not differ significantly between Pcdhg22 and Pcdhg0 retinas (Figure 2D,H,J).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data presented in Figure 2D,H,J.

claim: Pcdhgs are dispensable for formation of SAC–SAC synapses.
source: Thus, Pcdhgs are dispensable for formation of SAC–SAC synapses.
evidence: This claim is an inference based on the experimental data showing similar connectivity at P15-24 in Pcdhg22 and Pcdhg0 retinas.

claim: Synapses between closely spaced SACs were retained in Pcdhg0 mutants during the period that they were lost from controls.
source: In adults, in contrast, the pattern of SAC–SAC connectivity differed between Pcdhg22 and Pcdhg0 mice. Synapses between closely spaced SACs were retained in mutants during the period that they were lost from controls (Figure 2E,G,I,K).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data presented in Figure 2E,G,I,K.

claim: The loss of proximal SAC-SAC connections was selective in that the frequency and size of connections between SACs separated by >100 µm did not differ significantly between Pcdhg22 and Pcdhg0 mice.
source: This loss of proximal connections was selective in that the frequency and size of connections between SACs separated by >100 µm did not differ significantly between Pcdhg22 and Pcdhg0 mice (Figure 2J,K).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data presented in Figure 2J,K.

claim: Pcdhgs are required for synapse elimination between closely spaced SACs.
source: These results reveal a requirement of Pcdhgs for synapse elimination.
evidence: This claim is an inference based on the experimental data showing that proximal connections persist in Pcdhg0 retinas.

claim: Autaptic currents were elicited in ∼75% of Pcdhg0 SACs at P21-24, but in no Pcdhg22 SACs.
source: These stimuli elicited autaptic currents in ∼75% of Pcdhg0 SACs at P21-24, but in no Pcdhg22 SACs (Figure 3B,C).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data presented in Figure 3B,C.

claim: Autaptic currents resembled SAC–SAC connections in their latencies and rise times, were blockable by application of 50 µM picrotoxin, and averaged ∼20 pA in size.
source: Autaptic currents resembled SAC–SAC connections in their latencies and rise times, were blockable by application of 50 µM picrotoxin, and averaged ∼20 pA in size (Figure 3F,G and Figure 3—figure supplement 1B,C).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data presented in Figure 3F,G and Figure 3—figure supplement 1B,C.

claim: Autapses persisted into adulthood in Pcdhg0 SACs with sizes and frequency similar to those observed at P21-24.
source: Autapses persisted into adulthood in Pcdhg0 SACs with sizes and frequency similar to those observed at P21-24 (Figure 3D–G).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data presented in Figure 3D–G.

claim: One role of Pcdhg-mediated self-avoidance is to prevent formation of autapses.
source: Thus, one role of Pcdhg-mediated self-avoidance is to prevent formation of autapses.
evidence: This claim is an inference based on the experimental data showing autapses in Pcdhg0 but not Pcdhg22 SACs.

claim: The overall morphology, number, and spacing of SACs, as well as overall retinal structure, were normal in Pcdhg1 mice.
source: The overall morphology, number, and spacing of SACs, as well as overall retinal structure, were normal in Pcdhg1 mice (Figure 4A and Figure 2—figure supplements 3, 4)
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data presented in Figure 4A and Figure 2—figure supplements 3, 4.

claim: The frequency of SAC–SAC connections in Pcdhg1 mice was ∼20% of that in Pcdhg22 or Pcdhg0 mice.
source: The frequency of SAC–SAC connections in Pcdhg1 mice was ∼20% of that in Pcdhg22 or Pcdhg0 mice (Figure 4F).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data presented in Figure 4F.

claim: Current sizes in connected pairs in Pcdhg1 mice were on average ∼40% of those recorded in Pcdhg22 or Pcdhg0 mice.
source: Similarly, current sizes in connected pairs in Pcdhg1 mice were on average ∼40% of those recorded in Pcdhg22 or Pcdhg0 mice (Figure 4H).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data presented in Figure 4H.

claim: Forcing expression of the same Pcdhg isoform in all SACs decreased their connection strength to <10% of controls.
source: Thus, forcing expression of the same Pcdhg isoform in all SACs decreased their connection strength to <10% (0.2 × 0.4) of controls.
evidence: This claim is an inference based on the experimental data showing reduced frequency and current size in Pcdhg1 SACs.

claim: Pcdhg diversity is required for functional connectivity between neighboring SACs.
source: We conclude that Pcdhg diversity is required for functional connectivity between neighboring SACs.
evidence: This claim is an inference based on the experimental data showing reduced connectivity in Pcdhg1 SACs.

claim: SACs received strong excitatory inputs in Pcdhg22, Pcdhg0, and Pcdhg1 mice, with no significant differences among them.
source: SACs received strong excitatory inputs in Pcdhg22, Pcdhg0, and Pcdhg1 mice, with no significant differences among them (Figure 5B,C).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data presented in Figure 5B,C.

claim: Sizes of both ON and OFF inhibitory responses to spot flashes in vDSGCs were indistinguishable across the three genotypes.
source: Sizes of both ON and OFF inhibitory responses to spot flashes were indistinguishable across the three genotypes (Figure 5D,E).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data presented in Figure 5D,E.

claim: Excitatory spot flash responses in vDSGCs were unaffected by manipulation of Pcdhgs in SACs.
source: Similarly, excitatory spot flash responses in vDSGCs were unaffected by manipulation of Pcdhgs in SACs (Figure 5F,G).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data presented in Figure 5F,G.

claim: Pcdhg expression in SACs is dispensable for their ability to form and maintain synapses with other cell types.
source: Thus, Pcdhg expression in SACs is dispensable for their ability to form and maintain synapses with other cell types.
evidence: This claim is an inference based on the experimental data showing normal bipolar-SAC and SAC-DSGC connectivity in mutants.

claim: In all conditions, the ON and OFF dendrites of vDSGCs stratified in the ON and OFF SAC plexus, fasciculated with SAC dendrites, and maintained their modest structural asymmetry.
source: In all conditions, the ON and OFF dendrites of these DSGCs stratified in the ON and OFF SAC plexus, fasciculated with SAC dendrites, and maintained their modest structural asymmetry (Figure 5H–J).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data presented in Figure 5H–J.

claim: Altering Pcdhg expression in SACs had no detectable effect on the morphology of vDSGCs.
source: Thus, altering Pcdhg expression in SACs had no detectable effect on the morphology of vDSGCs.
evidence: This claim is an inference based on the experimental data showing normal vDSGC morphology in mutants.

claim: vDSGCs in Pcdhg22 mice exhibited strong ON and OFF directional responses.
source: vDSGCs in Pcdhg22 mice exhibited strong ON and OFF directional responses (Figure 6A) as shown previously (Kim et al., 2010; Trenholm et al., 2011; Duan et al., 2014).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data presented in Figure 6A and citations to prior literature.

claim: Direction selectivity of vDSGCs was diminished in both Pcdhg0 and Pcdhg1 retinas.
source: Direction selectivity of vDSGCs was diminished in both Pcdhg0 and Pcdhg1 retinas but in different ways.
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data presented in Figure 6.

claim: The average magnitude of the DSI vector was significantly decreased in Pcdhg0 retinas by ∼50% and in Pcdhg1 retinas by ∼35%.
source: In both genotypes, the average magnitude of the DSI vector was significantly decreased with respect to controls (by ∼50% in Pcdhg0 and ∼35% in Pcdhg1; Figure 6C–G).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data presented in Figure 6C–G.

claim: Responses of vDSGCs in Pcdhg0 retinas exhibited a significantly greater scatter around the ventral axis than those in wild-type retinas.
source: In contrast, responses of vDSGCs in Pcdhg0 retinas exhibited a significantly greater scatter around the ventral axis than those in wild-type retinas, whereas vDSGCs in Pcdhg1 retinas were as precisely tuned to ventral motion as controls (Figure 6C–F,H and Figure 6—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data presented in Figure 6C–F,H and Figure 6—figure supplement 1.

claim: vDSGCs in Pcdhg1 retinas were as precisely tuned to ventral motion as controls.
source: In contrast, responses of vDSGCs in Pcdhg0 retinas exhibited a significantly greater scatter around the ventral axis than those in wild-type retinas, whereas vDSGCs in Pcdhg1 retinas were as precisely tuned to ventral motion as controls (Figure 6C–F,H and Figure 6—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data presented in Figure 6C–F,H and Figure 6—figure supplement 1.

claim: The variance in preferred direction likely reflects the contorted morphology of SAC dendrites in Pcdhg0 but not Pcdhg1 retinas.
source: This variance likely reflects the contorted morphology of SAC dendrites in Pcdhg0 but not Pcdhg1 retinas.
evidence: This claim is an inference based on the experimental data and prior knowledge of SAC morphology in these mutants.

claim: The variation between the preferred direction of ON and OFF responses was greater in Pcdhg0 retinas than in either Pcdhg22 or Pcdhg1 retinas.
source: Likewise, the variation between the preferred direction of ON and OFF responses was greater in Pcdhg0 retinas than in either Pcdhg22 or Pcdhg1 retinas, indicating that SAC morphology and connectivity are disrupted independently in the ON and OFF SAC layers (Figure 6I).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data presented in Figure 6I.

claim: SAC morphology and connectivity are disrupted independently in the ON and OFF SAC layers in Pcdhg0 retinas.
source: Likewise, the variation between the preferred direction of ON and OFF responses was greater in Pcdhg0 retinas than in either Pcdhg22 or Pcdhg1 retinas, indicating that SAC morphology and connectivity are disrupted independently in the ON and OFF SAC layers (Figure 6I).
evidence: This claim is an inference based on the experimental data showing greater variation in Pcdhg0 retinas.

claim: vDSGCs in Pcdhg22 (control) retinas were most ventrally selective, followed by those in Pcdhg1 retinas; vDSGCs in Pcdhg0 retinas were the least selective.
source: vDSGCs in Pcdhg22 (control) retinas were most ventrally selective, followed by those in Pcdhg1 retinas; vDSGCs in Pcdhg0 retinas were the least selective (Figure 6J).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data presented in Figure 6J.

claim: Manipulating Pcdhg expression in SACs degrades the direction selectivity of DSGCs.
source: Together, these results demonstrate that manipulating Pcdhg expression in SACs, and thereby attenuating self-avoidance or S/NSD, degrades the direction selectivity of DSGCs.
evidence: This claim is an inference based on the experimental data showing reduced direction selectivity in mutants.

claim: Direction-selective responses are already present at eye opening in mice but become more selective with age.
source: Previous studies have shown that direction-selective responses are already present at eye opening in mice but become more selective with age (Elstrott et al., 2008; Yonehara et al., 2011; Chan and Chiao, 2013; Chen et al., 2014).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to prior literature.

claim: Direction selectivity of vDSGCs improved with age in control retinas but not in Pcdhg0 retinas.
source: We confirmed the improved age-dependent directional tuning of DSGCs in control retinas. In contrast, direction selectivity of vDSGCs did not improve in Pcdhg0 retinas (Figure 6—figure supplement 2).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data presented in Figure 6—figure supplement 2.

claim: Developmental refinement in SAC–SAC connectivity contributes to age-dependent improvement in direction selectivity.
source: This result is consistent the idea that developmental refinement in SAC–SAC connectivity contributes to age-dependent improvement in direction selectivity.
evidence: This claim is an inference based on the experimental data showing lack of improvement in Pcdhg0 retinas.

claim: Inhibitory input to DSGCs is greater for movement in the null direction than for movement in the preferred direction, whereas excitatory input is similar for movement in both directions.
source: First, inhibitory input to DSGCs is greater for movement in the null direction (dorsal for vDSGCs) than for movement in the preferred direction (ventral for vDSGCs), whereas excitatory input is similar for movement in both directions (Figure 7A,J,K).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data presented in Figure 7A,J,K and citations to prior literature.

claim: Excitatory and inhibitory currents recorded from DSGCs arise at the same time when motion is in the null direction, whereas inhibitory currents lag with respect to excitatory currents when motion is in the preferred direction.
source: Second, excitatory and inhibitory currents recorded from DSGCs arise at the same time when motion is in the null direction, whereas inhibitory currents lag with respect to excitatory currents when motion is in the preferred direction (Figure 7B,L,M).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data presented in Figure 7B,L,M and citations to prior literature.

claim: Both contributors to direction selectivity (asymmetric inhibition and timing) were blunted in Pcdhg0 and Pcdhg1 retinas.
source: We found that both of these contributors to direction selectivity were blunted in Pcdhg0 and Pcdhg1 retinas (Figure 7D,E,G,H and Figure 6—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data presented in Figure 7D,E,G,H and Figure 6—figure supplement 1.

claim: Inhibitory currents were larger for ventral motion and smaller for dorsal motion in Pcdhg0 and Pcdhg1 retinas than in Pcdhg22 retinas, with no significant change in excitation.
source: First, inhibitory currents were larger for ventral motion and smaller for dorsal motion in Pcdhg0 and Pcdhg1 retinas than in Pcdhg22 retinas, with no significant change in excitation (Figure 7J,K).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data presented in Figure 7J,K.

claim: The delay of inhibition in response to preferred motion was less in Pcdhg0 and Pcdhg1 retinas than in Pcdhg22 retinas, with no significant change for movement in the null direction.
source: Second, the delay of inhibition in response to preferred motion was less in Pcdhg0 and Pcdhg1 retinas than in Pcdhg22 retinas, with no significant change for movement in the null direction; in this case, Pcdhg0 and Pcdhg1 retinas were equally affected (Figure 7L,M).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data presented in Figure 7L,M.

claim: The ability of inhibition to veto excitation for preferred motion was greater in Pcdhg0 and Pcdhg1 retinas than in Pcdhg22 retinas.
source: Thus, the ability of inhibition to veto excitation for preferred motion was greater in Pcdhg0 and Pcdhg1 retinas than in Pcdhg22 retinas.
evidence: This claim is an inference based on the experimental data showing altered timing and magnitude of inhibition.

claim: The differences in the size and timing of inhibitory currents in vDSGCs from Pcdhg0 and Pcdhg1 retinas likely result in the changes in spiking observed.
source: It is likely that the differences in the size and timing of inhibitory currents in vDSGCs from Pcdhg0 and Pcdhg1 retinas result in the changes in spiking observed in Figure 6.
evidence: This claim is an inference based on the experimental data linking inhibitory currents to spiking behavior.

claim: Self-avoidance serves to optimize coverage of a receptive field by a dendritic arbor, minimizing gaps and clumps.
source: Morphological studies led to the idea that self-avoidance serves to optimize coverage of a receptive field by a dendritic arbor, minimizing gaps, and clumps (Kramer and Kuwada, 1983; Kramer and Stent, 1985; Grueber and Sagasti, 2010).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to prior literature.

claim: Self-avoidance prevents formation of autapses in SACs.
source: Our physiological studies revealed an additional role of self-avoidance in SACs: it prevents formation of autapses (Figure 3).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data presented in Figure 3.

claim: In many neuronal types, autapses cannot form because pre- and postsynaptic machinery are confined to axons and dendrites, respectively, which are physically segregated.
source: In many neuronal types, autapses cannot form because pre- and postsynaptic machinery are confined to axons and dendrites, respectively, which are physically segregated.
evidence: This is established knowledge about neuronal organization.

claim: SACs form dendro-dendritic synapses and have pre- and postsynaptic specializations intermingled.
source: SACs, in contrast, form dendro-dendritic synapses, and therefore have pre- and postsynaptic specializations intermingled.
evidence: This is established knowledge about SAC biology.

claim: Self-avoidance may play similar roles in other cells with intermingled pre- and postsynaptic specializations.
source: We suggest that self-avoidance may play similar roles in other such cells.
evidence: This is a speculation based on the findings in SACs.

claim: S/NSD is generally viewed as a means of limiting inter-dendritic repulsion to sibling processes, so that neurons of a single type can share territory.
source: S/NSD is generally viewed as a means of limiting inter-dendritic repulsion to sibling processes, so that neurons of a single type can share territory (Grueber and Sagasti, 2010; Zipursky and Grueber, 2013; Lefebvre et al., 2015).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to prior literature.

claim: In the retina, S/NSD additionally allows formation of synapses between SACs.
source: In the retina, it additionally allows formation of synapses between SACs.
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data in Figure 4.

claim: Several types of neurons have been shown to form homotypic connections in cortex and cerebellum.
source: Several types of neurons have been shown to form homotypic connections in cortex and cerebellum (Pfeffer et al., 2013; Rieubland et al., 2014).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to prior literature.

claim: Cortical fast-spiking interneurons, which form homotypic connections, also form autapses.
source: Indeed, cortical fast-spiking interneurons, which form homotypic connections, also form autapses (Bacci et al., 2003).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to prior literature.

claim: Connections between closely spaced SACs are selectively lost as the retina matures.
source: We also discovered two additional features of these connections. First, in mature retina (>P40), SACs separated by less than 100 µm seldom formed synapses with each other, whereas SACs separated by > 100 µm were connected frequently. Since dendritic overlap is inversely proportional to the distance between SACs, this distance-dependence is not a passive consequence of proximity but instead implies spatial selectivity to SAC–SAC connections. Second, we found that this distance-dependence was absent in immature retinas (P15-24; eye opening occurs at P14). Thus, connections between closely spaced SACs are selectively lost as the retina matures.
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data in Figure 2.

claim: The loss of proximal SAC–SAC connections is synapse elimination.
source: We view the loss of proximal SAC–SAC connections as synapse elimination, a process that occurs in many and perhaps most neuronal types (Kano and Hashimoto, 2009) but has not previously been described for SACs.
evidence: This claim is an inference based on the experimental data and knowledge of synapse elimination in other systems.

claim: Connections between closely spaced SACs are not eliminated in the absence of Pcdhgs.
source: We also found that connections between closely spaced SACs are not eliminated in the absence of Pcdhgs, revealing a novel role for these molecules in neural development.
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data in Figure 2.

claim: Strong SAC–SAC connectivity is critical for the developing visual system because it underlies propagation of retinal waves.
source: In fact, strong SAC–SAC connectivity is critical for the developing visual system, because it underlies propagation of the retinal waves that pattern the segregation of binocular input in retinorecipient areas such as the superior colliculus and lateral geniculate nucleus (Ford et al., 2012; Ackman and Crair, 2014; Burbridge et al., 2014).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to prior literature.

claim: Retinal waves occur before eye-opening.
source: Because waves occur before eye-opening, directional selectivity is unimportant.
evidence: This is established knowledge about retinal development.

claim: Postponing distance-dependent elimination of SAC–SAC connections until after eye-opening allows both the dense connectivity needed for wave propagation and the selective anti-parallel connectivity needed for direction selectivity.
source: Thus, we suggest that postponing distance-dependent elimination of SAC–SAC connections until after eye-opening allows both the dense connectivity needed for wave propagation and the selective anti-parallel connectivity needed for direction selectivity.
evidence: This is a speculation based on the experimental findings and knowledge of retinal development.

claim: The direction selectivity of DSGCs increases during the period in which connections between closely spaced SACs are being eliminated.
source: Consistent with this view, the direction selectivity of DSGCs increases during the period in which connections between closely spaced SACs are being eliminated.
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data in Figure 6—figure supplement 2.

claim: Anti-parallel inhibitory connections between SACs decrease the currents that SAC dendrites would otherwise provide to DSGCs during preferred motion through inhibition of inhibition.
source: In addition, anti-parallel inhibitory connections between SACs decrease the currents that these dendrites would otherwise provide during preferred motion (Figure 7C).
evidence: This claim is an inference based on the circuit model and experimental data.

claim: The number of SAC–SAC connections is markedly decreased in Pcdhg1 retinas.
source: The number of SAC–SAC connections is markedly decreased in Pcdhg1 retinas (Figure 7I).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data in Figure 4.

claim: In Pcdhg0 retinas, parallel SAC dendrites remain connected and inhibit each other, resulting in decreased inhibitory input from SACs to DSGCs for null motion and increased SAC–DSGC inhibition for preferred motion.
source: These connections persist in Pcdhg0 retinas, but their efficacy is decreased because parallel SAC dendrites remain connected and inhibit each other, resulting in decreased inhibitory input from SACs to DSCGs for null motion and decreased antiparallel SAC–SAC inhibition (and thus increased SAC–DSCG inhibition) for preferred motion (Figure 7F).
evidence: This claim is an inference based on the circuit model and experimental data.

claim: Autapses in Pcdhg0 retina would act similarly to synapses between parallel dendrites.
source: The autapses in Pcdhg0 retina would act similarly to synapses between parallel dendrites, since autapsing dendrites are likely to point in similar directions (see Pcdhg0 SAC image in Figure 3).
evidence: This claim is an inference based on the circuit model and morphological observations.

claim: Anti-parallel SAC–SAC connections transiently suppress transmitter release from SACs to DSGCs, contributing to delayed inhibition for preferred motion.
source: A recent computational model argues that the delayed inhibition for preferred motion arises in part because anti-parallel SAC–SAC connections transiently suppress transmitter release from SACs to DSGCs (Taylor and Smith, 2012).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to prior literature.

claim: Decreased inhibition from loss of SAC–SAC connections in Pcdhg1 retinas and decreased efficacy of SAC–SAC synapses in Pcdhg0 retinas would decrease the delay of inhibition, thereby blunting the response to preferred motion.
source: Decreased inhibition, from loss of SAC–SAC connections in Pcdhg1 retinas and decreased efficacy of SAC–SAC synapses Pcdhg0 retinas, would thus be expected to decrease the delay, thereby blunting the response to preferred motion.
evidence: This claim is an inference based on the circuit model and experimental data.

claim: The spatial organization of SAC–SAC inhibition and SAC–DSGC inhibition work together to generate a direction-selective output from the retina.
source: In summary, the spatial organization of SAC–SAC inhibition and SAC–DSGC inhibition work together to generate a direction-selective output from the retina.
evidence: This claim is an inference based on the experimental data and circuit model.

claim: When self-avoidance, S/NSD, or synapse elimination is perturbed, SAC–SAC inhibition is rendered less effective and direction selectivity is degraded.
source: When self-avoidance, S/NSD, or synapse elimination is perturbed, SAC–SAC inhibition is rendered less effective and direction selectivity is degraded.
evidence: This claim is an inference based on the experimental data.

claim: SAC–SAC connections play important roles in computation of direction selectivity.
source: Thus, our results demonstrate roles for these Pcdhg-dependent processes in computation of direction selectivity and provide new evidence in support of the hypothesis (Lee and Zhou, 2006; Enciso et al., 2010; Taylor and Smith, 2012; Vaney et al., 2012) that SAC–SAC connections play important roles in this computation.
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data and citations to prior literature.
